q: The G1 has nv = 35 and nu = 29. What do the six missing motors correspond to?
choices: The floating pelvis: no motor to the world
The two ankles, which are passive springs
The six arm joints that are left unpowered
The quaternion's extra numbers stored in qpos
why: 35 − 29 = 6 freedoms with no motor: exactly the pelvis's free joint. The quaternion explains nq = 36 vs nv = 35, a different count.

q: A robot has one free joint and 12 hinges, and a motor on every hinge. How many of its freedoms have no motor?
why: nv = 6 + 12 = 18 and nu = 12, so 6 are unactuated: the free joint's three translations and three rotations. 7 is the free joint's qpos count (quaternion), not its freedoms.

q: Why can't the G1's 29 motors, on their own, move the robot as a whole?
choices: Internal forces come in equal and opposite pairs
They are position servos, and a position servo cannot produce any force
They are too slow, at 500 Hz, to move the whole robot's mass
They can, but only while both feet are off the ground
why: Every motor pushes one link against another inside the robot; summed over the body, those pairs cancel. Only an external force, the floor's, changes the CoM's motion.

q: Summing F = ma over every link, which equation is left for the centre of mass c?
choices: m c̈ = f_floor + m g
m c̈ = Σ motor forces + m g
m c̈ = f_floor − Σ motor forces
m c̈ = m g only
why: Internal motor forces cancel in pairs, leaving only the floor's contact force and gravity. That is why the floor is the only thing that can move the body horizontally.

q: Which statement about moving the G1's body horizontally is correct?
choices: Only the floor; motors just change how it pushes
The hip motors push the CoM forward directly, as hard as they like
Gravity alone moves it, since gravity is the only external force
The free joint carries a motor that moves the pelvis forward
why: m c̈ = f_floor + m g: gravity is purely vertical, motors are internal. The robot can only move its legs so that the floor pushes the body where it wants.

q: A foot stands on the floor. Which force can the floor exert on it?
choices: A push only, where the foot touches, within friction
A push or a pull, whichever the ankle servo commands
Any force at all, as long as the foot is flat on the ground
A downward pull whenever the robot starts to lean too far
why: The floor can push, never pull, only where a foot touches it, and sideways only as hard as friction allows. These rules are what make the CoP stay inside the support polygon.

q: How does the course describe walking?
choices: Deliberately falling and catching yourself
Holding the CoM still while the legs move
Pushing the body forward with the hip motors
Keeping the CoM over a foot at every instant
why: Lean so gravity carries the body forward, let the stance foot's force steer it, then put the next foot where it catches the fall. Keeping the CoM over a foot at all times is static walking.

q: Which describes static walking?
choices: CoM over each foot before the other lifts; slow but stable frozen
CoM between the feet, falling toward the next one; fast, and frozen it falls
CoM held at the midline the whole time; both feet always on the ground
CoM swinging outside both feet; stable only at high speed
why: Static walking keeps the robot balanced at every instant by parking the CoM over the stance foot. The second option is dynamic walking.

q: A dynamically walking robot is frozen mid-step. What happens?
choices: It falls: its CoM is between the feet, over no foot
It stays up: the ZMP plan was inside the polygon
It stays up as long as the servos hold the pose
It falls only if double support was removed
why: Dynamic walking spends most of its time with the CoM over no foot, falling toward the next one. It is fast and efficient precisely because it uses the fall; frozen, nothing catches it.

q: What is the centre of pressure (CoP)?
choices: The force-weighted mean of the contact points
The plain, unweighted average of the contact points
The point directly below the centre of mass
The contact point carrying the largest force
why: p = Σ fᵢxᵢ / Σ fᵢ: many small upward forces act like one force of size Σ fᵢ at p. It is below the CoM only when the robot is not accelerating horizontally.

q: Two contacts: 300 N at x = 0 and 100 N at x = 0.2 m. Where is the CoP?
why: p = (300·0 + 100·0.2)/400 = 0.05 m, pulled toward the heavier contact. 0.10 m is the unweighted midpoint; 0.15 m swaps the weights.

q: Three contacts: 100 N at x = 0, 100 N at x = 0.1 m, 200 N at x = 0.2 m. Where is the CoP?
why: Σfx = 0 + 10 + 40 = 50 N·m over Σf = 400 N gives 0.125 m. 0.100 m is the unweighted mean of the three positions.

q: Feet at y = −0.12 m and y = +0.12 m. All weight is on the right foot (y = −0.12), the left carries 0 N. Where is the CoP?
choices: y = −0.12 m, at the loaded foot
y = 0, at the midline
y = −0.06 m, halfway
y = +0.12 m, at the unloaded foot
why: With weight 1 on one contact and 0 on the other, the weighted average is that contact. The midline answer ignores the forces.

q: Can the CoP leave the convex hull of the contact points if one contact pushes very hard?
choices: No: non-negative weights summing to 1 keep it inside
Yes: a large enough force drags the CoP beyond that contact point
Yes, but only in single support, when there are fewer contacts
No, but only because the controller clips it back inside
why: However big one force gets, its weight approaches 1 and the CoP approaches that contact, never past it. Leaving the hull would need a negative weight: a floor that pulls.

q: What is the zero moment point (ZMP)?
choices: Where gravity plus inertia give no tipping moment
The point on the floor directly below the centre of mass
The point where the ankle servo torque is exactly zero
The floor point where the vertical contact force is zero
why: It is defined by zero moment about horizontal axes from gravity plus the body's inertia. It is below the CoM only when the CoM is not accelerating.

q: How are the ZMP and the CoP related on flat ground?
choices: The same point, computed from motion or from forces
The ZMP is always ahead of the CoP by the step length
The CoP is the ZMP projected onto the support polygon
They coincide only when the robot is standing still
why: On flat ground ZMP = CoP: the ZMP comes from the motion, the CoP from the contact forces. That is what lets the walker measure its ZMP from MuJoCo's contact forces.

q: What is the balance rule for flat feet?
choices: The ZMP must be inside the support polygon
The CoM must be inside the support polygon
The capture point must be at the midline
The ZMP must be outside the stance foot
why: A motion that needs the ZMP outside the polygon cannot happen with flat feet. The CoM itself may be outside (dynamic walking); it is the ZMP that is constrained.

q: A planned motion would need the ZMP outside the support polygon. What happens with flat feet?
choices: The foot rolls on its edge; no ankle torque stops it
The ZMP moves outside and the robot balances anyway
The floor pulls down on the heel to keep the foot flat
Friction holds the foot flat as long as μ > 0.2
why: The ZMP cannot leave the polygon, since the floor only pushes. If the motion needs it outside, the foot tips about its edge instead.

q: What is the support polygon in single support and in double support?
choices: One foot's outline; the convex hull of both feet
Both feet's outline; the stance foot only
A circle under the CoM; the line joining both ankles
The stance foot's heel; the two toes only
why: Support polygon = convex hull of the contact points. In single support that is one small foot; in double support the hull around both feet.

q: How big is one G1 foot's support polygon?
choices: About 17 × 6 cm
About 30 × 12 cm
About 10 × 10 cm
About 24 × 4 cm
why: Four contact spheres at x ∈ {−0.05, +0.12} m and y ≈ ±0.025 to 0.03 m: 17 cm by about 6 cm, to balance a 33.3 kg robot.

q: Which assumptions define the linear inverted pendulum model (LIPM)?
choices: Point mass at the CoM, massless leg to p, constant CoM height z_c
Rigid body with full inertia, massless feet, constant leg length
Point mass at the CoM, massive legs, CoM height that bobs freely
Two point masses, one per leg, joined by a spring at the hip
why: All mass in one point, a massless leg from it to the floor at p, and constant height. Constant height is what makes the model linear; a constant leg length would give the ordinary nonlinear pendulum.

q: In the LIPM derivation, what does constant CoM height give?
choices: f_z = m g: the vertical floor force equals the weight
f_x = m g: the horizontal force equals the weight
f_z = 0: the floor carries no vertical force
ẍ = 0: the CoM cannot accelerate horizontally
why: Constant height means z̈ = 0, so Newton vertically gives f_z − m g = 0. The horizontal force is what drives ẍ.

q: Why must the floor force point along the massless leg, so that f_x/f_z = (x − p)/z_c?
choices: A massless leg cannot carry a moment
Friction is zero, so only normal forces act
The servos hold the leg at a fixed angle
Gravity acts along the leg's direction
why: A massless link transmitting a moment would get infinite angular acceleration, so the force runs along it, from p to the mass. Its components are then in the ratio of the leg's sides.

q: LIPM with m = 30 kg, g = 10 m/s², z_c = 0.6 m, and the CoM 0.06 m ahead of the ZMP. What is the horizontal floor force?
choices: 3 N
why: f_x = m g (x − p)/z_c = 300 × 0.06/0.6 = 30 N. 300 N is the vertical force; 18 N forgets to divide by z_c.

q: What is the LIPM's equation of motion for the CoM's horizontal position x?
choices: ẍ = ω²(x − p), with ω = √(g/z_c)
ẍ = −ω²(x − p), with ω = √(g/z_c)
ẍ = ω²(x − p), with ω = g/z_c
ẍ = ω(x − p), with ω = √(z_c/g)
why: m ẍ = m g (x − p)/z_c. The minus sign would make it a spring (a valley); ω = g/z_c forgets the root and has the wrong units.

q: The LIPM is ẍ = ω²(x − p). Which picture fits it?
choices: A hill: it accelerates away from p, more when further
A valley: the CoM is pulled back toward p and settles there
A spring: the CoM oscillates about p at frequency ω
A ramp: the CoM accelerates at a constant g regardless of x
why: The acceleration has the same sign as x − p, so any offset grows: an inverted pendulum. Reading it as a spring is the sign error the professor warns about.

q: Why is the ZMP called the "zero moment" point in the LIPM?
choices: m z_c ẍ = m g (x − p) says the net moment about p is zero
The ankle servo applies zero torque at the stance foot
The CoM has zero angular momentum about the hip
Gravity's moment about the CoM is always zero
why: Multiply m ẍ = m g (x − p)/z_c by z_c: gravity's moment about p equals the inertial force's moment. It is an equation of motion from a moment balance, not a torque.

q: What are the units of ω = √(g/z_c)?
choices: m/s
s
m/s²
why: g/z_c is (m/s²)/m = 1/s², so ω is in 1/s and 1/ω is a time.

q: LIPM with ω = 5 /s and the CoM 0.04 m ahead of the ZMP. What is ẍ?
choices: 1 m/s², away from the ZMP
1 m/s², toward the ZMP
0.2 m/s², away from the ZMP
25 m/s², away from the ZMP
why: ẍ = ω²(x − p) = 25 × 0.04 = 1 m/s², with the sign of x − p: away. 0.2 forgets to square ω; "toward" is the valley misconception.

q: A LIPM has z_c = 0.4 m (take g = 10 m/s²). What are ω and the time constant 1/ω?
choices: ω = 5 /s, time constant 0.2 s
ω = 25 /s, time constant 0.04 s
ω = 0.2 /s, time constant 5 s
ω = 5 /s, time constant 5 s
why: ω = √(10/0.4) = √25 = 5 /s and 1/ω = 0.2 s. 25 forgets the square root; 0.2 /s inverts the ratio.

q: A robot's CoM height is multiplied by four. What happens to ω?
choices: It halves
It quarters
It doubles
It is unchanged
why: ω = √(g/z_c) ∝ 1/√z_c, and 1/√4 = 1/2. "Quarters" forgets the square root. A taller robot falls more slowly.

q: On a world with g = 1.6 m/s² and z_c = 0.4 m, what are ω and the time constant?
choices: ω = 2 /s, time constant 0.5 s
ω = 4 /s, time constant 0.25 s
ω = 0.5 /s, time constant 2 s
ω = 5 /s, time constant 0.2 s
why: √(1.6/0.4) = √4 = 2 /s, so 1/ω = 0.5 s: weaker gravity, slower fall. 5 /s is the Earth value for this height.

q: For the G1's LIPM with z_c = 0.60 m, what are ω and the time constant?
choices: ω = 4.04 /s, time constant 0.247 s
ω = 16.4 /s, time constant 0.061 s
ω = 1.64 /s, time constant 0.61 s
ω = 4.04 /s, time constant 0.65 s
why: √(9.81/0.6) = 4.04 /s, 1/ω = 0.247 s. 1.64 /s is the Moon value; 0.65 s is the step duration, not the time constant.

q: With p fixed, x(0) = x0 and ẋ(0) = v0, what is the LIPM solution?
choices: x(t) = p + (x0 − p) cosh ωt + (v0/ω) sinh ωt
x(t) = p + (x0 − p) cos ωt + (v0/ω) sin ωt
x(t) = p + (x0 − p) cosh ωt + v0 ω sinh ωt
x(t) = p + (x0 − p) sinh ωt + (v0/ω) cosh ωt
why: Trying e^(rt) gives r = ±ω, and the two initial conditions fix the cosh and sinh coefficients. cos/sin would be the spring (valley) solution; v0·ω has the wrong units.

q: How does the walking controller compute the LIPM CoM trajectory at 500 Hz?
choices: It evaluates the cosh/sinh closed form directly
It integrates ẍ = ω²(x − p) numerically with small steps
It looks the trajectory up in a table learned from data
It runs MuJoCo forward to predict where the CoM will go
why: The LIPM has an exact solution, so the controller just evaluates it at time sT. No numerical integration is needed anywhere.

q: In the LIPM, the CoM is released at rest exactly above the ZMP (x0 = p, v0 = 0). What happens?
choices: It stays put, but any offset would grow
It slides toward the nearer foot and stops there
It oscillates about p with period 2π/ω
It falls forward at once with acceleration g
why: x(t) = p for all t: an equilibrium, but on top of a hill. Any offset x0 − p grows like cosh ωt.

q: Released at rest with the CoM 2 cm from p, after a time where cosh ωt ≈ 7, how far is it from p?
choices: About 14 cm
About 2 cm
About 0.3 cm
About 9 cm
why: With v0 = 0, x − p = (x0 − p) cosh ωt = 0.02 × 7 = 0.14 m. The error multiplies; it does not add (9 cm would be 2 + 7).

q: A step lasts 0.6 s and ω = 5 /s. How many time constants long is the step?
why: 1/ω = 0.2 s, and 0.6/0.2 = 3 (= ωT). 0.12 is T/ω and 8.3 is ω/T, both upside down; 15 multiplies by ω².

q: With z_c = 0.6 m, a 0.65 s step is 2.6 time constants. By roughly how much does a starting error grow in one step?
choices: About ×7 (cosh 2.6)
About ×2.6 (one per τ)
About ×13 (e^2.6)
why: Released at rest, the distance from p grows like cosh ωT, and cosh 2.6 ≈ 7. 2.6 is the number of time constants, not the growth; e^2.6 ≈ 13 forgets that cosh is half of e^ωT plus a vanishing term.

q: A starting error grows about ×7 over each 0.65 s step. What does the professor conclude?
choices: That is why a walker must act every step
So errors average out if you take many steps
So longer steps let the error settle down
So the LIPM is of no use for real walking
why: Errors multiply, never settle: left alone for a step or two, any mistake is ×7, ×49. Longer steps make it worse, since growth is cosh ωT.

q: In the (x − p, ẋ) phase portrait, what happens on the line ẋ = −ω(x − p)?
choices: The CoM comes to rest exactly over p
The CoM runs away from p fastest
The CoM oscillates around p forever
The CoM crosses p and falls the other way
why: On that line only the e^(−ωt) part is present, so the CoM moves toward p at exactly the speed that stops it on top. ẋ = +ω(x − p) is the runaway line.

q: Starting anywhere off the rest line ẋ = −ω(x − p), what eventually happens to the LIPM?
choices: It runs away, to its side of the rest line
It settles back onto the rest line by itself
It runs away, always in the direction it was moving
It circles the origin of the phase plane forever
why: Every motion is a mix, and the e^(+ωt) part eventually wins. The side of the green line decides the direction of the fall, not the current velocity alone.

q: What is the capture point ξ?
choices: ξ = x + ẋ/ω: where to step to come to rest in one step
ξ = x − ẋ/ω: where to step to come to rest in one step
ξ = x + ẋ ω: where the CoM will be one step from now
ξ = p + ẋ/ω: how far the ZMP moves per time constant
why: ξ = x + ẋ/ω measures how far the state is from the rest line. x − ẋ/ω is the other combination η, which settles by itself.

q: The CoM is at x = 0, moving at 0.2 m/s, with ω = 4 /s. Where is the capture point?
choices: 0.05 m ahead
0.05 m behind
0.8 m ahead
0.2 m ahead
why: ξ = 0 + 0.2/4 = 0.05 m. Subtracting gives −0.05; multiplying by ω gives 0.8.

q: The CoM is at x = 0.1 m, moving at 0.5 m/s, with ω = 5 /s. Where is the capture point?
why: ξ = 0.1 + 0.5/5 = 0.2 m. x − ẋ/ω gives 0; x + ẋω gives 2.6; x + ẋ gives 0.6.

q: z_c = 0.4 m, g = 10 m/s², and the CoM moves at 0.3 m/s. How far ahead of the CoM is the capture point?
choices: 6 cm ahead
1.2 cm ahead
1.5 m ahead
6 cm behind
why: ω = √(10/0.4) = 5, so ẋ/ω = 0.3/5 = 0.06 m ahead. 1.2 cm uses ω = 25 (no root); 1.5 m multiplies by ω; behind is the x − ẋ/ω sign slip.

q: At one speed the capture point is 7.4 cm ahead of the CoM. The robot doubles its speed (same ω). Where is it now?
choices: About 15 cm ahead
About 7.4 cm ahead
About 30 cm ahead
About 10.5 cm ahead
why: ξ − x = ẋ/ω is linear in ẋ, so doubling the speed doubles it. 30 cm would be quadratic; 10.5 cm (×√2) has no basis.

q: The capture point obeys ξ̇ = ω(ξ − p). What does that mean?
choices: First order, and ξ − p grows like e^(ωt)
A second-order equation: ξ oscillates about p at frequency ω
A first-order equation: ξ decays onto p on its own
No dynamics at all: ξ is a constant of the motion
why: ξ(t) − p = (ξ0 − p)e^(ωt): the unstable part of the LIPM isolated in one variable. The combination that decays by itself is η = x − ẋ/ω.

q: ξ0 − p = 1 cm with p held fixed. After one time constant 1/ω, how far is ξ from p?
choices: About 2.7 cm
About 2 cm
About 1 cm
About 7 cm
why: ξ − p = (ξ0 − p)e^(ωt), and at t = 1/ω that is e ≈ 2.7 times. 7 is cosh 2.6, the per-step growth, not per time constant.

q: The foot (the ZMP) is put exactly on the capture point ξ. What happens?
choices: ξ stays put, and the CoM slides onto it and stops
The CoM stops at once, wherever it happens to be
The CoM runs away from ξ as fast as possible
The CoM oscillates around ξ until damping stops it
why: With p = ξ, ξ̇ = ω(ξ − p) = 0, so ξ is fixed and the state lies on the rest line. The CoM coasts onto the foot and comes to rest.

q: A robot steps well beyond its capture point. What happens, according to the LIPM?
choices: It is pushed back: the CoM stops short
It is safest: stepping further is always better
It stops exactly over the new foot
It keeps falling forward past the foot
why: Step short and you keep falling forward; step beyond and you are pushed back. Only stepping on ξ brings the CoM to rest in one step.

q: At 0.3 m/s with ω = 4.04 /s, where is the capture point, and what changes at twice the speed?
choices: 7.4 cm ahead; at twice the speed ~15 cm, more than the foot reaches
15 cm ahead; at twice the speed ~30 cm, more than the foot reaches
7.4 cm ahead; at twice the speed still within the 17 cm foot
1.2 cm ahead; at twice the speed 2.4 cm, inside the foot
why: 0.3/4.04 = 7.4 cm. Twice the speed needs ~15 cm, beyond the ~12 cm the foot reaches ahead of the ankle, so you must take a step.

q: How does the walker choose a step's initial CoM velocity v0?
choices: Solve a BVP so x(T) = x_T: exactly one answer
Integrate the LIPM backwards in time from the end of the step
Try several v0 values on the robot and keep the best one
Set v0 to the capture point so the step ends at rest
why: x_T = p + (x0 − p) cosh ωT + (v0/ω) sinh ωT is linear in v0, so it has one solution. No search or trial and error is needed.

q: The professor says to "run it backwards" to plan a step. What does that mean?
choices: Reason from the end you want to the start you need
Integrate the LIPM equation backwards in time
Play the recorded motion in reverse to check it
Walk the robot backwards to test its stability
why: It means the boundary value problem: fix x(T) and solve for v0. It is not integrating backwards in time.

q: With z_c = 0.6 m, the CoM must go from −0.07 m to +0.07 m in 0.65 s over a fixed ZMP. What v0 did the BVP give?
why: 0.14 m in 0.65 s averages 0.215 m/s, but the pendulum slows the CoM until it passes the foot, so it must start faster: 0.327 m/s. 0.416 m/s is the sideways v0.

q: How are the per-step boundary value problems combined into a gait?
choices: Chained: each step starts exactly where the last one ended
Solved independently, each from the robot's starting point
Averaged, so that every step uses the same v0
Solved once for the first step and then repeated
why: Each step's CoM trajectory must start where the previous one ended. Computing them absolutely breaks the continuity at every support exchange.

q: The robot falls at every support exchange, and the commanded pelvis jumps back half a stride there. What is the cause?
choices: Bookkeeping: steps computed absolutely, not chained
A balance problem: the ZMP leaves the support polygon at exchange
A damping problem: λ in the leg IK is too small
A gravity problem: ω is too large for this CoM height
why: Computing each step's trajectory absolutely teleports the body back half a stride. It looks like a balance failure and is bookkeeping.

q: For mirrored sideways steps (stance foot at ±w), where is the CoM at each support exchange?
choices: Exactly on the midline, y0 = 0
Directly over the new stance foot
Directly over the old stance foot
Halfway between midline and foot
why: Solving the periodic boundary problem forces y0 = −y0, so y0 = 0: the CoM crosses the midline at each support exchange, moving toward the new stance foot.

q: For the G1's sideways sway (w = 0.119 m), what are v0 at exchange and the sway's peak?
choices: v0 = 0.416 m/s, peak 5.9 cm
v0 = 0.327 m/s, peak 11.9 cm
v0 = 0.416 m/s, peak 11.9 cm
v0 = 0.110 m/s, peak 2.5 cm
why: v0 = ω w tanh(ωT/2) = 0.416 m/s, and the sway peaks at 5.9 cm. 0.327 m/s is the forward BVP's v0.

q: In the G1's periodic sway, does the CoM reach the foot it leans toward?
choices: No: it peaks at 5.9 cm against the foot at 11.9 cm
Yes: it must be over the foot to be balanced
Yes, but only during double support
No: it never leaves the midline at all
why: It never reaches the foot. Requiring the CoM over the foot is static walking; the dynamic gait only needs the ZMP there.

q: The swing foot follows x = x_A + (x_B − x_A)(σ − sin 2πσ / 2π). Why that shape?
choices: Its speed factor 1 − cos 2πσ is 0 at both ends
It is the shortest path from x_A to x_B
It keeps the foot speed constant all the way
It makes the foot accelerate fastest at landing
why: Zero velocity at σ = 0 and σ = 1: the foot leaves gently and lands at rest. A straight line would jump to full speed at once.

q: Why not swing the foot along a straight line, x_A + (x_B − x_A)σ?
choices: It starts at full speed and lands still sliding
It is just as good; the cycloid only looks nicer
It is too slow to finish within one step
It makes the foot rise too high at mid-swing
why: A linear blend has constant speed from the first instant: a jolt the servos cannot follow and a foot still moving when it lands.

q: Swing height z = z0 + h(1 − cos 2πσ)/2 with h = 0.10 m. How high above z0 is the foot at σ = 0.25?
choices: 0 m

q: Double-support fraction d = 0.20 at each end, swing fraction σ = (s − d)/(1 − 2d). What is σ at step fraction s = 0.35?
Which is the walker's pipeline, run every cycle at 500 Hz?
choices: Time → step → LIPM CoM target → foot targets → DLS IK → 29 servos → physics
IMU → state estimate → LIPM CoM target → foot targets → DLS IK → servos
Time → DLS IK → LIPM CoM target → foot targets → 29 servos → physics
Contact forces → ZMP → capture point → foot targets → 29 servos → physics
why: It is open loop: nothing comes back from the physics, no IMU, no measured ZMP. The IK comes after the CoM and foot targets, since it turns them into angles.

q: What are the walker's default gait parameters?
choices: Step 0.14 m, 0.65 s, clearance 0.10 m, 20 % double support
Step 0.65 m, 0.14 s, clearance 0.20 m, 10 % double support
Step 0.14 m, 0.45 s, clearance 0.10 m, no double support
Step 0.30 m, 0.65 s, clearance 0.05 m, 50 % double support
why: 0.14 m strides, 0.65 s per step, 10 cm swing clearance, 20 % double support at each end. 0.45 s steps are the rushed gait that falls.

q: Why is the walker's first step only a half stride?
choices: Both feet start level, so a full stride would over-reach
The LIPM needs one half step to measure ω
The servos must warm up before full strides
The capture point starts behind the heels
why: Each later forward BVP runs from half a stride behind the stance foot to half ahead. Starting with feet level, the first step only needs to cover half.

q: Someone pushes the walking G1 sideways mid-walk. What does the analytic walker do?
choices: Nothing different: it is open loop and never reads the IMU
It steps onto its new capture point to catch itself
It shifts its ZMP with ankle torque to recover
It slows its gait until the sway dies away
why: The walker never measures where the body is; it cannot see the push, so it cannot react. Catching it would need feedback, e.g. capture-point stepping.

q: Which list gives the open-loop walker's limitations?
choices: Drifts sideways, no push recovery, flat ground, fixed gait
Slips on ice, needs learning, cannot turn, drains the battery
Too slow to compute, singular at the crouch, falls on the Moon
Needs an IMU, needs a camera, needs 150 million steps
why: Nothing pulls it back, nothing reacts to disturbances, and the gait is fixed at design time. Ice (friction 0.2) actually changes nothing for this gait.

q: Why did the field move from planned walkers like this one to feedback?
choices: A plan made in advance is brittle outside its conditions
Because the LIPM mathematics turned out to be wrong
Because analytic walkers cannot walk at all in practice
Because learned policies need far fewer simulation steps
why: The maths works, as the walker shows; but an open-loop plan cannot respond to pushes, drift or terrain. Learned policies need far more steps (~150 million), not fewer.

q: Why can the ZMP not jump instantly from one foot to the other?
choices: Non-negative weighted average: between feet only while both touch
The servos are too slow to shift the weight from one foot to the other in a single cycle
The LIPM forbids any change of p within a step, since p is held fixed in the solution
The CoM must first pass over the new foot, and that takes one whole time constant
why: With only one foot touching, all the weight is there; the ZMP can travel between the feet only during double support. That is why the gait spends 20 % of each step there.

q: Is double support essential for the G1 walker, or just a nicety?
choices: Essential: with double_support = 0 it falls at 2.0 s
A nicety: it only makes the gait look smoother
Harmful: removing it makes the gait more stable
Irrelevant: the ZMP can switch feet instantly
why: Without it the ZMP must switch feet in an instant, the step starts with an error, and errors grow ×7 per step. Measured: a fall at 2.0 s.

q: How far and how fast did the analytic G1 walker go?
choices: 0.99 m in 8.8 s, about 0.11 m/s
8.8 m in 0.99 s, about 9 m/s
0.65 m in 8.8 s, about 0.07 m/s
0.99 m in 2.0 s, about 0.5 m/s
why: Walked 0.99 m in 8.8 s with no learning and ~200 lines of code: 0.99/8.8 ≈ 0.11 m/s. 2.0 s is when the no-double-support gait falls.

q: What made the week 4 G1 walk?
choices: One linear ODE, its exact solution, a cycloid and IK
A neural network policy trained for 150 million simulation steps
A reward function tuned by search in MuJoCo over many runs
Motion-capture data from human walkers, replayed through IK
why: No training, no data, no reward function: roughly two hundred lines of analytic control (Layer 4) doing the whole job.

q: Within what band did the G1's pelvis height stay during the walk?
why: The crouched gait kept the pelvis in 0.69–0.74 m throughout, and it ended upright at 0.716 m. A lower band would mean a deep squat; the 0.13 m figure is a collapsed robot.

q: When did the failure variants of the walker fall?
choices: No double support 2.0 s; rushed 3.2 s; Moon 5.3 s; ice never
No double support 5.3 s; rushed 2.0 s; Moon 3.2 s; ice 8.8 s
No double support 3.2 s; rushed 5.3 s; Moon 2.0 s; ice never
All four fell at the first support exchange, about 1.0 s
why: Measured with walk.py: double_support = 0 at 2.0 s, 0.45 s steps at 3.2 s, Moon gravity at 5.3 s; ice (friction 0.2) changes nothing for this gait.

q: The walker is put on ice (friction 0.2) without telling the controller. What happens?
choices: Nothing changes for this gait
It slips and falls at the first step
It falls at 2.0 s, like no double support
It walks, but only half as far
why: Measured: ice (friction 0.2) changes nothing for this gait. Friction only caps how hard the floor can push sideways, and this gait stays within that cap.

q: On the Moon (g = 1.62 m/s², z_c = 0.6 m), ω ≈ 1.6 /s instead of 4.04 /s. How does the time constant change?
choices: About 2.5 times longer: ~0.6 s instead of 0.25 s
About 2.5 times shorter: ~0.1 s instead of 0.25 s
About 6 times longer: ~1.5 s instead of 0.25 s
Unchanged: the time constant depends only on z_c
why: 1/ω goes from 0.247 s to about 0.61 s, a ratio of √(9.81/1.62) ≈ 2.5. 6 is the ratio of the g values, which forgets the square root.

q: The measured ZMP leaves the support polygon while the G1 walks. What does the course conclude?
choices: The ZMP criterion is right; the LIPM's assumptions failed
The ZMP criterion is wrong for real humanoid robots
The contact-force measurement must have a bug in it
The robot is about to fall, since the ZMP is outside
why: Theory says flat feet cannot put the ZMP outside; the real robot breaks the model's assumptions (swinging leg, bobbing CoM, heavy legs, rolling feet, sagging servos). Teach it; do not "fix" it.

q: Over the walk, where did the measured ZMP y range, against stance feet at ±0.119 m?
why: From about −0.23 to +0.11 m, beyond the −0.119 m foot on one side. −0.12 to +0.10 m is just one early step's row from the printout.

q: Which real-robot fact breaks the LIPM's massless-leg assumption?
choices: About 30 % of the G1's mass is below the hips
The servos have finite stiffness and sag
The CoM bobs as the stance leg compresses
The weight rolls across a finite-size foot
why: All four are listed failures, but only the heavy legs contradict "massless legs". Sagging servos break rigid control, bobbing breaks constant height, rolling breaks instant exchange.

q: Complete the professor's line: "A model does not have to be true to be useful, only …"
choices: … wrong in ways that do not matter yet.
… simple enough to solve by hand.
… right on average over many steps.
… tuned on the real robot's data.
why: The LIPM is wrong about the G1 in five ways and the robot still walks. Weeks 11 and 12 are where those errors start to matter.

q: A learned walking policy may need 150 million simulation steps. What does the course say learning buys?
choices: Robustness, not the gait itself
The gait itself, which analytic control cannot produce
Speed: learned gaits are always faster to compute
Nothing that analytic control cannot match
why: An analytic controller already walks in ~200 lines with no data. "Learning buys robustness, not the gait itself."
